introduction.text: The Fontana dell'Acqua Acetosa is a historic fountain in Rome's Parioli quarter, known for its iron‑rich water that was celebrated by Pope Paul V for its medicinal properties and for being a popular monument among Italians.

history.description: In the 16th century, the Romans discovered the ferruginous water known as acqua acetosa flowing in the area.
In 1613, Pope Paul V had the water analyzed and found it to be drinkable and curative for various diseases.
In 1619, Pope Paul V commissioned architect Giovanni Vasanzio to build a fountain at the site.
In 1663, the profession of selling the water, called acquacetosari, was first mentioned.
In 1712, Pope Clement XI commissioned a restoration of the fountain, addressing low water flow and quality issues.
In 1821, stone seats were installed at the fountain thanks to funding from Ludwig I of Bavaria.
In 1959, the fountain was closed due to aquifer pollution and later reopened with water from the mains.
In 2003, the Fondo Ambiente Italiano identified the fountain as the monument Italians are most fond of.
Between 2008 and 2009, the fountain underwent significant renovation and a small fenced park was created.

design.description: The fountain features a tympanum with the papal coat of arms, a staircase leading downwards, and an exedra‑shaped façade with three niches displaying the Chigi family coat of arms.
The design is attributed to Andrea Sacchi or Marco Antonio De 'Rossi, not to Gian Lorenzo Bernini.

art.description: The niches of the fountain display the Chigi family coat of arms, showing six mountains and an eight‑pointed star.
The tympanum above the fountain bears the papal coat of arms.
